title: Congresswoman Escobar Honors El Pasoans During Commendation Ceremony
text:
Tonight, Congresswoman Veronica Escobar (TX-16) will be hosting her fourth Congressional Commendation Ceremony, recognizing a group of outstanding El Pasoans whose work has strengthened the community across fields including education, public service, the arts, science, and advocacy.

“It is a privilege as our community’s federal representative to recognize the strength, resilience, and talent of our honorees,” said Congresswoman Escobar. "El Paso is grateful for their contributions and we are proud to celebrate the profound impact each of these individuals has made on our beloved community."

Information on each of the honorees (listed in alphabetical order) can be found below:

Beatriz Landin created the Wander Pillow, a neck pillow with a blanket stored inside that was featured on Amazon Prime Video’s “The Blox”.

Blueberry Carrillo gained national recognition by winning the prestigious Dav Pilkey Silver Medal Portfolio Award in June. She was one in twelve in the nation selected and the only student from Texas to receive the award in the Art category.

El Dorado High School’s “The Legend” yearbook staff was named a Columbia Scholastic Press Association Gold Crown Award recipient in 2024 for its 2023 yearbook “Como Cuando”.

Jose Hurtado, Ph.D is a UTEP professor in the Department of Earth, Environmental and Resource Sciences and a member of NASA’s Artemis II and II Science Teams. He earned a prestigious grant through the Lunar Mapping Program, supported by NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey to create high-quality, modern geologic maps of the moon.

Karime Lopez is student leader and innovator in STEM education. In May, she won the FIRST Leadership Award at the 2026 FIRST Robotics World Championship.

Manuela Alejandra Gomez, Ph.D. was appointed as one of only 12 internationally recognized scholars to serve as an advisor and research associate for the Moses Mesoamerican Archive and Research Project at Harvard University.

Marco Sanchez is a student at Harmony School of Innovation is a STEM driven civic leader from El Paso, Texas and is the Founder and President of Harmony Robotics Organization. He founded the El Paso Youth Alliance, a student run organization with the mission to help young people participate in civic engagement and local government. He is an alumni of Congresswoman Escobar’s Congressional Youth Advisory Council.

Margie Salazar became CEO of FirstLight, the first woman CEO of a local major credit union. In March, she was named the 2026 Remarkable Woman for El Paso, a program is designed to spotlight women who lead, inspire and forge a path for others in their communities.

Noel Candelaria is a special education teacher in Ysleta Independent School District. He currently serves as Vice President of the National Education Association, the nation's largest labor union representing more than three million educators.

Retired Command Sergeant Major Janina Simmons made history in 2019 as the first Black woman to graduate from the U.S. Army Ranger School. Her accomplishments also include becoming an ultramarathon runner and a published author.

Shaheli De Silva is a student at Young Women’s STEAM Research and Preparatory Academy. Earlier this year, she won the Regional English Spelling Bee in English and tied for first in EPISD’s Spanish Spelling Bee.

title: Franklin Leads Members Of Florida Delegation In Effort To Protect Domestic Fertilizer Production
text:
Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18) led members of Florida’s congressional delegation in a letter to President Trump and Commerce Secretary Lutnick urging continued action to address the supply and rising cost of sulfur, a critical input used to produce phosphate fertilizer.

“Florida is at the heart of America’s phosphate fertilizer production, and the current sulfur shortage threatens an industry our farmers and food supply depend on,” said Congressman Scott Franklin. “A reliable, affordable supply of sulfur is critical to producing fertilizer American farmers depend on. I appreciate the Trump Administration’s work on this issue, and we want to build on those efforts to protect American fertilizer production, support our farmers and reduce our dependence on foreign sources.”

Geopolitical and shipping disruptions have constrained global sulfur supplies and driven prices to historic levels. Tampa sulfur prices have risen sharply from a previous average of $172 per long ton. Since May, prices have exceeded $1,100 per metric ton. This increase has put significant pressure on domestic phosphate fertilizer production.

Domestic phosphate producers have already reduced operating rates and idled facilities as sulfur costs and supply constraints have intensified. Further disruptions could threaten American jobs, tighten fertilizer supplies, increase costs for farmers and leave the United States more dependent on foreign fertilizer.

The Trump Administration has convened an interagency process to examine the issue. Franklin and his colleagues encouraged continued engagement and outlined potential options to increase access to competitively priced sulfur, including coordination with domestic refiners and sulfur marketers, addressing transportation and logistics constraints, using appropriate trade and financing tools and engaging allied suppliers.

The lawmakers also encourage the Administration to designate a senior official to coordinate the federal response and work with Congress on any additional authorities or resources that may be needed.

Cosigners include: Reps. Byron Donalds (FL-19), Kat Cammack (FL-03), Daniel Webster (FL-11), Gus Bilirakis (FL-12), Laurel Lee (FL-15), Greg Steube (FL-17) and Anna Paulina Luna (FL-13).

Read the full letter here.

title: Reps. Gabe Evans, Lou Correa Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Improve Transparency of SBA Spanish-Language Resources
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Reps. Gabe Evans (R-CO-08), Lou Correa (D-CA-46), Monica De La Cruz (R-TX-15), Henry Cuellar (D-TX-28), Maria Elvira Salazar (R-FL-27), Jim Costa (D-CA-21) and David Valadao (R-CA-22), introduced the bipartisan SBA Spanish Resource Report Act, legislation to give Congress and the public a clearer picture of the Spanish-language resources currently available to entrepreneurs and small business owners through the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA).

This legislation ensures that Congress and Spanish-speaking entrepreneurs are aware of the resources and services that remain available to them through the SBA.

“As the grandson of Mexican immigrants and the representative of a district with a prominent Hispanic community, I know the critical role Hispanic small businesses play in our economy. This bill directs an inventory to be conducted of existing Small Business Administration Spanish-language resources to provide greater clarity to Congress and small business owners across our country regarding what resources and services are currently available.” –– Congressman Gabe Evans (R-CO-08)

"Hispanic Americans own more than five million businesses across this country, employing nearly three million workers. Everyone in this great nation who’s willing to work hard and contribute deserves a fair shot at the American Dream, and this bill is a step in that direction. The SBA Spanish Resource Act is common-sense legislation that makes sure Spanish-speaking small business owners and entrepreneurs have the resources they need to succeed.” — Congressman Lou Correa (D-CA-46)

"Language should never be a barrier to success. With over one million Hispanic-owned small businesses in Texas, I am proud to join bipartisan legislation that expands access and awareness of Spanish-language tools at the SBA. Our small businesses are the backbone of our communities, and I will continue working to ensure Texas main streets thrive.” — Congresswoman Monica De La Cruz (R-TX-15)

“For many small business owners in South Texas, Spanish is the language they use every day with their families, employees, and customers. Federal resources should be accessible to the people they are meant to serve, and this bipartisan bill will help make sure the SBA understands where language gaps may be making it harder for our small businesses to get the information they need.” — Congressman Henry Cuellar (D-TX-28)

“In South Florida, small business happens in both English and Spanish. That is why Congress should know what Spanish-language resources the SBA already offers, how they are being used, and what they cost. I am proud to introduce the SBA Spanish Resource Report Act, to give Congress the information it needs to oversee these resources responsibly and make sure they are serving the small-business owners they are meant to help.” — Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar (R-FL-27)

“Across the San Joaquin Valley, small businesses drive our local economy, including thousands of entrepreneurs who conduct business in Spanish. They deserve clear information about the resources available through the SBA. This bipartisan legislation gives Congress the facts we need to identify gaps in the availability of Spanish-language materials and make sure these resources are reaching the communities they are intended to serve.”— Congressman Jim Costa (D-CA-21)

“Small businesses are the backbone of communities across the Central Valley, and every entrepreneur should be able to access the information and resources they need to succeed—no matter what language they speak. In the past, the Small Business Administration has provided some resources in multiple languages, but many of those translations have now been removed altogether. With over 74% of CA-22’s population identifying as Hispanic, there are countless native Spanish-speaking small business owners who rely on accessible information to start, grow, and sustain their businesses. I’m proud to support the bipartisan SBA Spanish Resource Report Act to ensure Congress has the information necessary to understand whether these entrepreneurs have meaningful access to the resources they need to succeed.” — CongressmanDavid Valadao (R-CA-22)

The SBA Spanish Resource Report Act requires the SBA Administrator to provide Congress with a one-time report within 180 days detailing existing Spanish-language resources and services offered through SBA programs. The report must also be made publicly available on the SBA’s website.

Specifically, the report would examine Spanish-language websites, application materials, guidance documents, outreach materials, and customer service resources. It would also review resources available through SBA partners, including Small Business Development Centers, Women’s Business Centers, SCORE chapters, and Veteran Business Outreach Centers.

Where data is available, SBA would also report on how these resources are being used, geographic trends, associated translation and administrative costs, operational considerations, and recommendations for efficiently administering existing Spanish-language services.

Importantly, the bill does not require the SBA to create, expand, reduce, or eliminate any Spanish-language resource or service. Instead, it gives Congress greater transparency into what already exists so lawmakers can make informed decisions based on facts.

Background

In December 2025, SBA removed certain Spanish-language materials from its website, raising concerns about the availability of information for Spanish-speaking entrepreneurs. SBA has continued to provide some Spanish-language resources and services.

Hispanic-owned businesses are an important part of America’s small-business economy. The bipartisan SBA Spanish Resource Report Act seeks to establish a clear, public accounting of the resources SBA currently provides and ensure Congress has the information necessary to conduct effective oversight.

The legislation also requires the SBA Administrator to brief the House and Senate Small Business Committees within 30 days after submitting the report.

title: Garbarino Applauds Reappointment of Dr. John Howard to Lead World Trade Center Health Program
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Andrew R. Garbarino (NY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security, today congratulated Dr. John Howard on his reappointment to another six-year term as Director of the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) and Administrator of the World Trade Center Health Program (WTCHP).

The reappointment comes just days before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks and follows a bipartisan, bicameral letter led by Garbarino and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand urging Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to retain Dr. Howard. In July, Garbarino and Gillibrand led 26 bipartisan Members of Congress in calling for his reappointment.

“For more than two decades, Dr. Howard has been a trusted advocate for the 9/11 community and dedicated leader of the World Trade Center Health Program,” said Congressman Garbarino. “As we mark 25 years since September 11th, I am grateful that Dr. Howard will continue this important work and congratulate him on his six-year reappointment. I thank President Trump and Secretary Kennedy for making this reappointment possible and for recognizing the importance of Dr. Howard's experienced leadership. Responders and survivors deserve stability, certainty, and a Program that will be there for them for years to come. I look forward to continuing to work with Dr. Howard to make sure they receive the care and support they have earned.”

Dr. Howard was first appointed Director of NIOSH in 2002 and has served in the role under administrations of both parties. As NIOSH Director, he also serves as Administrator of the World Trade Center Health Program, which provides medical monitoring and treatment to more than 140,000 9/11 responders and survivors nationwide.

Earlier this year, Garbarino helped secure lifetime funding for the World Trade Center Health Program. He has continued working with members of the 9/11 community to ensure the Program has the staffing, resources, and leadership necessary to provide care for responders and survivors suffering from 9/11-related illnesses.

In their July letter, Garbarino, Gillibrand, and their colleagues emphasized that Dr. Howard's continued leadership would provide stability and institutional knowledge as the Program enters its next chapter.

title: Congressman Vicente Gonzalez Announces $2.5 Million in Federal Funding for City of Brownsville Public Works
text:
Contact: Alexis Torres

Brownsville, Texas – Today, Congressman Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34) announced $2.5 million in federal funding for the City of Brownsville Public Works Department to support the design and construction of the Marina Industrial Park, including roadway, water, sewer and stormwater infrastructure. The funds are delivered through the U.S. Economic Development Administration (EDA) and estimated to create 590 new jobs and leverage over $18 million in private investment. The total projected cost of this project is $4,395,000.

“Brownsville has quickly become a prime attraction for American manufacturers and businesses to call our city home. We must have the transportation and infrastructure in place to meet these heightened demands for economic growth. This funding helps us get there while creating hundreds of new jobs and bringing millions of dollars in new opportunities to the Rio Grande Valley. When we invest in local development, we invest in the future of South Texas,” said Congressman Gonzalez.

“Brownsville is attracting new industries, creating quality jobs, and strengthening its role as a leading hub for international trade and manufacturing. This $2.5 million federal investment in the Marina Industrial Park will further support our effort to build the critical infrastructure needed to support that growth, while leveraging more than $18 million in private investment and creating new jobs. We are grateful to Congressman Gonzalez and the U.S. Economic Development Administration for recognizing Brownsville’s economic potential and investing in our community’s future,” said Mayor John Cowen, Jr., City of Brownsville.

The Marina Industrial Park will include five state-of-the-art multi-tenant industrial buildings: four buildings of 150,000 square feet each and one slightly smaller facility of 140,000 square feet. Located on FM 511 in Brownsville’s northern industrial corridor, the new Industrial Park is an ideal gateway for manufacturers to supply goods across North America as it is near two interstate highways, four international bridges, the Port of Brownsville, three international airports, and a U.S.-Mexico rail crossing.

title: RELEASE: Ahead of the 25th Anniversary of 9/11, Gottheimer Announces More Than $5 Million in Federal Funds to Combat Terrorism
text:
Above: Gottheimer unveils 9/11 legislation package.

NEW MILFORD, NJ — Today, Wednesday, September 9, 2026, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) announced several concrete actions including more than $5 million clawed back from Washington to Jersey for local law enforcement in North Jersey to combat terrorism.

Watch Gottheimer’s remarks here.

The new funding will go toward expanding and modernizing intelligence and coordination, officer training, and additional resources to protect Jersey families.

The resources include:

More than $5 million in counterterrorism funding clawed back for local law enforcement across Bergen, Sussex, and Passaic Counties.

Every single town — all 65 in the Fifth Congressional District — in Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties — will receive $50,000 to be utilized for counter-terrorism training.

$1.5 million dollars for Bergen County to expand and modernize the Bergen County Real-Time Intelligence Center.

Newton in Sussex County will receive $200,000 in funding to be able to purchase a real-time intelligence platform to enhance its capabilities.

Bloomingdale will receive $100,000 to purchase a response drone and active-threat gear — ballistic shields, armor, breaching kits.

Vernon will receive $30,000 in funding for a thermal search-and-overwatch drone for fast response at any time of day or conditions.

Highlighted the bipartisan 9/11 Review Task Force Report that lays out twenty bipartisan recommendations for the Intelligence Community to protect against the new and emerging threats — including faster information sharing between agencies, adopting AI to stay ahead of our enemies, and deeper partnerships with our state, local, and private-sector partners to fight terror.

Sent a letter pressing the FAA and Secretary Duffy to fully implement secondary flight deck barriers on all commercial aircraft — the only 9/11 Commission recommendation still not fully implemented 25 years later — to require the barriers on every plane, including older aircraft already flying. In 2018, I wrote the bipartisan Saracini Aviation Safety Act, requiring these barriers on all new aircraft and it was signed into law in 2018. Years later, the FAA still hasn’t finalized the rule to retrofit the existing fleet.

Introduced a 9/11 education bill with Congresswoman Elise Stefanik (NY-21) to ensure that 9/11 is taught in every school across America. Only 15 states require 9/11 education.

Introduced a resolution, cosponsored by every member of the New Jersey House congressional delegation, formally recognizing the state’s law enforcement officers, firefighters, and emergency medical personnel who responded to the World Trade Center attacks and carried out the rescue, recovery, and relief efforts in the days and months that followed. The resolution honors their service and sacrifice, remembers those who have since died — including from 9/11-related illnesses — and reaffirms the federal commitment to the World Trade Center Health Program and the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund.

“We all have a responsibility, in honor of those who gave their lives, and for the sake of our democracy, to teach our children, our students, and our future leaders the history of our homeland,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “Today, I unveiled a package of federal action that lays out a series of steps we must take to not only honor those who perished on 9/11 and in its aftermath, but to be prepared to stop any future attacks. With today’s actions, we will keep fighting to protect our state, our homeland, and ensure that a tragic day like that one in September of 2001 never happens again.”

Gottheimer was joined by Bergen County Prosecutor Mark Musella, Sussex County Prosecutor Dan Perez, New Milford Mayor Michael Putrino, New Milford Councilwoman Lisa Sandhusen, New Milford Councilwoman Randi Duffie, New Milford Councilman Matt Seymour, Bloomingdale Councilman David Bronkhurst, Newton Police Chief Dan Finkle, Vernon Mayor Anthony Rossi, Vernon Police Chief Daniel Young, Sussex County Chief of Detectives Nicholas T. Elmo, Sussex County Lieutenant Kyle Phlegar, Sussex County Detective Andrew Moore, Bergen County Executive Jim Tedesco, Bergen County Commissioner Germaine Ortiz.

Below: Gottheimer unveils 9/11 legislation package.

Gottheimer’s remarks as prepared for delivery:

Good morning, everyone.

Twenty-five years ago, this week, New Milford lost one of its own.

Stephen Dorf (DOOR-F) was 39 years old. He worked as a communications technician for Euro Brokers, on the 84th floor of the South Tower.

Stephen was one of six kids in a close-knit family from Brooklyn, and by every account I’ve read, he was exactly the kind of guy you’d want as a neighbor and friend. He was the neighbor grilling in the backyard, the guy who’d give you the shirt off his back if you needed it. That’s who New Milford and Jersey lost on September 11, 2001. Not a statistic. Not a name on a wall. A friend from this remarkable community and our great state.

The steel beam behind us from the towers, the plaque, this plot of land — they mean something. Because behind them is a piece of New Milford’s story that this town will never be torn down.

Because of 9/11, and the havoc monsters wreaked that day, we have memorials like this one across our state and country. I’ve prayed at beautiful memorials like this one more times than I can count over the years. They are both powerful remembrances of our loved ones, a reminder of the strength of our democracy and the flag we pledge to, the indefatigable will of our people, and, in our hours of need, our ability to come together as a nation.

Last week, I was at memorials at the Pentagon, in Lower Manhattan, in Shanksville — and every time, I think about the same thing: the people we lost and their families.

The nearly 3,000 souls that day, and the 750 who called New Jersey home. One hundred and forty-seven from Bergen County alone.

I think about the passengers on Flight 93, who fought back over a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, so that plane never reached its target — the United States Capitol. They literally came together and voted, on the spot, to swap their lives for the terrorists — to protect us.

I think about the more than 400 first responders who ran into those towers instead of running away — because that’s what they do, and that’s what they still do, every day, right here in New Milford.

And I think about something that doesn’t get said enough: more than 9,000 first responders and survivors have died from illnesses tied to what they breathed in at Ground Zero. That is three times the number of people who died on the day of the attack itself. I think about the 60,000 servicemen and women who gave their lives in or were injured in the War on Terror in Iraq and Afghanistan.

For those of us who lived through this tragedy, where we were and how we learned about the attacks is seared in our memory. But, twenty-five years is a long time.

It’s long enough that we have college students graduating this spring who weren’t alive for 9/11. We have educators in our classrooms who weren’t alive. 100 million Americans have been born since that tragic morning — nearly a third of our country. Their only connection to that day is a memorial like this one, a story from their parents, a paragraph in a textbook, if they’re lucky enough to get a paragraph at all.

So, when we say never forget, we all have a responsibility, in honor of those who gave their lives, and for the sake of our democracy, to teach our children, our students, our future leaders the history of our homeland. Otherwise, TikTok will do it — and they may say what the most despicable people are posting and what some of our enemies are spreading — that 9/11 was our fault. I will do everything in my power, and I know you will, too, to ensure that our children learn the truth, honor the fallen, and protect the greatest country the world has ever known.

But that takes work. In 2004, the 9/11 Commission published a report with clear steps to help prevent another terror attack on our soil. As a result, Congress established the National Counterterrorism Center. We created the Director of National Intelligence. We built a system where our intelligence agencies can escape their silos and share information – it was one of the great weaknesses that contributed to the attack that day.

Twenty years later, there is still one 9/11 Commission recommendation — just one — that has never been fully carried out: secondary barriers, to keep terrorists out of the cockpit on every commercial flight in America. Many of us have been working on that for years – but we’re still not there, and there’s no excuse for the airlines’ failure to fully meet that demand. And, there is still work to be done to make sure threats are better shared between our intelligence agencies, especially as they develop faster and grow more sophisticated

As we’ve said, twenty-five years is a long time. America is facing new threats that didn’t exist in 2001, like Artificial Intelligence and the government of China.

For the past year, I served as Co-Chair of the House Intelligence Committee’s bipartisan 9/11 Review Task Force, with Congresswoman Elise Stefanik, Chairman Rick Crawford, and Ranking Member Jim Himes. We spent a year in hearings and briefings, grading our own government’s homework: how well did we actually carry out the original 9/11 Commission’s recommendations, what worked and what didn’t — and how do we prepare for the next generation of threats.

Our report [hold up a copy] lays out twenty bipartisan recommendations to close the gaps for the next 25 years. Things like faster information sharing between agencies, adopting AI to stay ahead of our enemies, and deeper partnerships with our state, local, and private-sector partners to fight terror.

Today, I want to lay out a series of steps we must take to not only honor those who perished on 9/11 and its aftermath, but to be prepared to stop any future attacks.

The first step starts here, in our communities, and it’s about ensuring that our towns and first responders have the resources they need to protect our families here in Bergen, Sussex, and Passaic Counties. This morning, I’m announcing $5 million in new federal counter-terrorism resources that I secured for every community in the Fifth District.

Every single town — all 65 in the Fifth Congressional District — in Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties — will receive $50,000 to be utilized for counter-terrorism training — to be prepared for any threats, especially the new ones. That’s $3.25 million in new training dollars.

That funding will allow our towns to receive advanced tactical training for responding to active shooters and violent threats. New specialized training will help identify and mitigate threats to our schools and houses of worship, and it will ensure the maximum number of officers can receive this crucial training without impacting day-to-day operations.

What worked twenty-five years ago doesn’t work today. We must invest in our first responders so they can protect themselves and our families.

In addition, to ensure we are prepared and coordinating, we are investing more than 1.5 million dollars here in Bergen County to expand and modernize the Bergen County Real-Time Intelligence Center. That’s the hub that connects more than 70 law enforcement, fire, and EMS agencies countywide — to better integrate and coordinate emergency response across the county.

The Intelligence Center ensures that agencies don’t miss a beat when a thief flees from one town to the next, and all hands will be on deck for major events at MetLife Stadium.

As part of the federal dollars I secured, Newton in Sussex County will be able to purchase a real-time intelligence platform and help existing systems that aren’t connected. Vernon will receive funding for a thermal search-and-overwatch drone for fast response at any time of day or conditions. And Bloomingdale will receive dollars to purchase a response drone and active-threat gear — ballistic shields, armor, breaching kits. Those are major tools — major federal investments — in the hands of the men and women who are the first on the scene when we need them most – to handle any major threat thrown at them, including terror.

My hope is that all of our communities and agencies will be able to work hand-in-hand, locally, seamlessly, across the state, and with federal partners. That is so critical and one of our biggest lessons from the original 9/11 report and our review.

Second, I’m sending an urgent letter to the FAA and Secretary of Transportation Duffy to finally finish the job on secondary cockpit barriers. Years ago, I wrote the bipartisan Saracini Aviation Safety Act, requiring these barriers on all new aircraft. It was signed into law in 2018.

I then helped pass legislation to require the barriers on every plane — including older aircraft already flying. Yet, years later, the FAA still hasn’t finalized the rule to retrofit the existing fleet. When it finally happens, it will take years to implement. We need the FAA to implement a final rule and get every plane in our skies equipped with a secondary cockpit barrier.

It makes no sense for flight attendants to drag a drink cart into the aisle when the pilot needs to leave the cockpit to use the restroom.

We know that won’t work if a terrorist wants it — studies show that they will literally push over the cart.

Third, I’m leading a resolution this week with the entire New Jersey Congressional House delegation formally honoring New Jersey’s 9/11 first responders. The cops, the firefighters, the EMTs who ran toward the towers, who searched the rubble for months afterward, drawn from all twenty-one of our counties. The ones who helped run the largest waterborne evacuation in American history, carrying an estimated half a million people to safety across the Hudson.

This resolution remembers them, and it reaffirms our commitment to funding the World Trade Center Health Program and the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund for as long as they’re needed.

Finally, this step addresses what I discussed at the beginning of my remarks. With my colleague Congresswoman Elise Stefanik of New York, I just introduced a bipartisan bill to ensure that 9/11 is taught in every classroom in America. Not on TikTok, but in our textbooks.

Why? Because if a generation of kids grows up not understanding what happened that day, and why, we haven’t just failed the memory of those lost. We’ve failed the future, we’ve our democracy, and our ability to protect our country. I will not let that happen. Only fifteen states have a requirement to teach about 9/11 – and, believe it or not, New Jersey isn’t one of them. We should change that today, and, in the meantime, I will fill that gap with bipartisan federal legislation.

Twenty-five years ago, I remember, like a lot of you probably do, watching President Bush stand on a pile of smoking rubble at Ground Zero, grab a bullhorn, and shout back to rescue workers who couldn’t hear him: “I can hear you. The rest of the world hears you.” Out of the worst morning in this country’s history, that’s what America decided to be — loud, united, and unafraid.

That’s the New Jersey I know. That’s the New Milford I know. A place where our memory and our pride outlast fear. A place where a guy named Stephen Dorf, who just wanted to go to work and come home to his family, will never, ever be forgotten.

With today’s actions — with real funding, a real report, and real legislation — with the best first responders in the country, the best service men and women, and intelligence officers in the world, we will keep fighting to protect our state, our homeland, and ensure that a tragic day like that one in September of 2001 never happens again.

Because in the greatest country in the world, I know that if we work together, our best days will always be ahead of us.

Thank you. God bless you, God bless our first responders, and God bless the United States of America.

title: RELEASE: Gottheimer Introduces Bipartisan Bill to Stop Rogue AI Agents and Keep People in Control
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Wednesday, September 9, 2026, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) and Congressman Mike Lawler (NY-17) introduced the bipartisan Stop Rogue AI Act to ensure businesses and federal agencies have the ability to see rogue and dangerous AI agents operating inside their own networks, and stop them before they cause real damage.

Right now, most organizations have no reliable way to know how many unauthorized AI agents are running in their systems, who built them, or what they have access to. AI agents can be activated by employees, embedded in third-party software, or deployed by vendors — often with little to no visibility for the organization whose networks they’re operating on to know that they are there. That blind spot is becoming more dangerous by the day. The recent Hugging Face incident and other autonomous cyberattacks have shown AI systems are being used to hack organizations at scale, without a person ever watching or stepping in.

“Right now, AI agents are running loose in our networks, and nobody can see them or verify who built them — making it increasingly hard to stop them,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “That’s a five-alarm security risk. We’ve already seen AI systems hack organizations on autopilot, with no person at the wheel. My bipartisan bill with Congressman Lawler puts humans back in the driver’s seat so we can find agents and know exactly who’s behind them so that organizations can effectively protect their systems.”

“AI agents are becoming more capable and more deeply integrated into our government and economy. We need to make sure we know what these systems are, what they can access, and who is responsible for them. We can harness the benefits of AI while making sure these systems don’t operate in the shadows of the networks they have access to,” said Congressman Mike Lawler (NY-17).

The Stop Rogue AI Act would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), to develop national standards, guidelines, and best practices for discovering, verifying, and controlling AI agents.

Under the bill, those standards will provide guidance to organizations on how to:

Find and track every AI agent operating on their systems, in a continuous, easily readable inventory;

Verify who built and operates each agent, using verifiable identity and provenance — not just a vendor’s word;

Monitor agents in real time, including detecting prompt injection, data theft, and agents behaving outside their approved limits; and

Allow, deny, or revoke an agent’s access, actions, and interactions at any time – so people have the final say over what it can access or do.

The bill also requires federal contractors and agencies to build these safeguards into how they buy and deploy AI agents, and directs NIST and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to fold the standards into existing federal cybersecurity guidance.

The bipartisan legislation has already earned support from a broad coalition spanning network security, internet infrastructure, and AI governance, including:

Palo Alto Networks

GoDaddy

Infoblox

AI Policy Network

Alliance for Secure AI

“As AI agents become more capable of acting and transacting on our behalf, identity and accountability are foundational. We need open, interoperable standards that make it possible to know which agent is acting, who stands behind it, and whether its credentials are valid. Representatives Gottheimer and Lawler’s bipartisan effort is an important step toward establishing those standards and putting them to work through federal adoption. GoDaddy is pleased to support an approach that can strengthen security while keeping the agentic web open to businesses and innovators of every size,” said Jared Sine, Chief Strategy & Legal Officer, GoDaddy.

“Securing AI agents starts with knowing they exist and being able to trust who they are. This bill rightly treats agent discovery as foundational cybersecurity, giving agencies the ability to continuously find, verify, and control the AI agents interacting with their systems. We’re especially encouraged that this legislation promotes open, vendor-agnostic, and interoperable discovery standards built on existing internet infrastructure like the domain name system, rather than locking agencies into proprietary platforms. That approach is scalable, resilient, and the right foundation for agent security. Reps. Gottheimer and Lawler are doing commendable work, and we look forward to supporting the bill’s advancement,” said Wei Chen, Chief Legal Officer and EVP, Regulatory Strategy, Infoblox

“As AI agents rapidly scale across government and enterprise systems, security and governance must evolve to address the novel risks of agentic decision-making. Palo Alto Networks applauds Representatives Josh Gottheimer and Mike Lawler for their bipartisan leadership in introducing the AI Agent Standardization and Security Act. This legislation provides a strong foundation for organizations to safely adopt agentic AI while maintaining continuous visibility, runtime monitoring, identity verification and control,” said Daniel Kroese, Vice President, Public Policy and Government Affairs, Palo Alto Networks

The Stop Rogue AI Act builds on Gottheimer’s work as Co-Chair of the House AI Commission and his bipartisan track record on AI safety and consumer protections. It comes as Congress and federal regulators face growing pressure to keep pace with the rapid development and deployment of autonomous AI systems.

###

title: RELEASE: Gottheimer, Stefanik Discuss Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses at Vanderbilt University, Launch New Bipartisan Caucus on Campus Antisemitism
text:
Above: Gottheimer announces Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus at Vanderbilt University.

NASHVILLE, TN — Today, Tuesday, September 8, 2026, Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) and Congresswoman Elise Stefanik (NY-21) announced the launch of the new bipartisan Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus while visiting Vanderbilt University. The caucus aims to hold colleges and universities accountable for protecting Jewish students, faculty, and staff.

The Representatives announced the formation of the caucus during a conversation at Vanderbilt University featuring Vanderbilt Chancellor Daniel Diermeier and five visiting university leaders from across the country, including leaders from The University of Kentucky, The University of Texas at Austin, Dartmouth College, The University of Alabama, and Washington University in St. Louis. The panel discussed how their campuses are working to combat antisemitism while protecting free expression.

“Since October 7th, Jewish students on too many campuses have been harassed, intimidated, and made to feel like strangers in their own school,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “That’s why Elise and I are teaming up to launch this caucus to hold universities accountable, back up the schools getting it right, like Vanderbilt, and make sure every Jewish kid can have a college experience without fear of discrimination or violence.”

“From asking questions at the most watched hearing in Congressional history with university presidents that led to an earthquake in higher education to passing key legislation, I have been proud to be the leader in Congress on combatting antisemitism and anti-Americanism at our colleges and universities,” said Congresswoman Elise Stefanik (NY- 21). “I am proud to launch this bipartisan Congressional Caucus with my friend and colleague Representative Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) who has been a leading partner and legislator with whom I have worked on this critical issue. We are committed to saving American higher education for the next generation.”

Since the October 7, 2023 Hamas terrorist attack on Israel, antisemitism on American college campuses has surged to levels never before recorded. According to the Anti-Defamation League, antisemitic incidents on campuses spiked more than 300 percent in 2023 alone, followed by a further sharp rise in 2024, with well over a thousand incidents logged in the year after October 7th. The vast majority of Jewish college students say they have personally witnessed or experienced antisemitism since that day.

The Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus will:

Serve as a bipartisan forum for Members of Congress to coordinate oversight of how colleges and universities respond to antisemitism.

Press institutions to protect Jewish students, faculty, and staff, and to enforce their own anti-harassment and anti-discrimination policies.

Advance and track federal legislation targeting campus antisemitism and BDS-driven discrimination, including the Antisemitism Awareness Act, the HEAL Act, and the newly House-passed Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act.

Spotlight schools that are getting it right and share best practices across campuses nationwide.

Gottheimer has been a leading voice in Congress against antisemitism, including:

Authoring the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which directs the Department of Education to use the IHRA working definition of antisemitism when enforcing federal anti-discrimination law. The bill passed the House 320–91 last Congress.

Helping pass the Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act, restricting federal student aid to colleges that engage in commercial BDS boycotts of Israel. The bill cleared the House 237–169 on September 3rd and now heads to the Senate.

Authoring the HEAL Act (Holocaust Education and Antisemitism Lessons Act) and the October 7th Remembrance Education Act to strengthen Holocaust and October 7th education in schools.

Leading H.Res. 883, declaring the “from the river to the sea” chant antisemitic, and the IGO Anti-Boycott Act, both of which have passed the House.

Pressing university presidents directly, sending letters to schools including Rutgers, Columbia, Harvard, Penn, MIT, Princeton, Brown, GW, and NYU demanding concrete plans to protect Jewish students.

Serving as a member of the House Bipartisan Task Force for Combating Antisemitism.

title: Congressman Harris Announces $6 Million USDA Investment in Invasive Catfish Processing
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Andy Harris, M.D. (MD-01), Chairman of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, today announced $6 million in U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) grant funding to expand processing capacity for invasive wild-caught catfish.

The funding, available through USDA Rural Development’s Meat and Poultry Processing Expansion Program, will provide grants of $50,000 to $2 million to help eligible processors expand facilities, purchase equipment, and increase invasive catfish processing capacity. Applications are due December 7, 2026, through Grants.gov.

Statement from Congressman Harris:

“Invasive blue catfish are reducing the blue crab and native fish populations that Maryland watermen harvest and sell. Increasing processing capacity will strengthen the market for wild-caught catfish, expand opportunities for watermen and seafood processors, and remove more invasive fish from the Bay. I thank Secretary Rollins and USDA for making this funding available to protect the Chesapeake Bay and strengthen Maryland’s seafood economy.”

title: Comisionado Impulsa Proyectos de Agua para Puerto Rico.
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — Como parte de su agenda para priorizar lo básico y atender la crisis de agua en Puerto Rico, el Comisionado Residente, Pablo José Hernández, solicitó al Senado que mantenga en la versión final de la legislación federal de infraestructura de agua varios proyectos y prioridades para Puerto Rico que ya fueron aprobados por la Cámara de Representantes.

Las prioridades ya están incluidas en la versión de la Ley de Desarrollo de Recursos Hídricos, conocida como el Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) de 2026 de la Cámara de Representantes, que avanzó en comité, y Hernández está trabajando para que se mantengan durante las negociaciones con el Senado y lleguen a la versión final.

“Mi agenda de priorizar lo básico se trata de conseguir resultados en los problemas que afectan a nuestra gente todos los días. Puerto Rico necesita mejor infraestructura de agua, comunidades más protegidas de las inundaciones y acción para nuestras costas. Ya estamos avanzando estas prioridades en la Cámara y ahora estoy trabajando para asegurar que lleguen a la meta,” expresó el Comisionado Residente.

Entre las medidas que el Comisionado Residente busca asegurar se encuentran hasta $75 millones para proyectos de infraestructura de agua y ambiental en Puerto Rico, $10 millones para agua y alcantarillado en Corozal y nuevos estudios de impacto para el proyecto de control de inundaciones del Río Puerto Nuevo en San Juan, de manera que se puedan atender las preocupaciones de las comunidades aledañas.

También está defendiendo nuevos estudios para proyectos de control de inundaciones, protección costera y daños por tormentas en Ceiba, Fajardo, Loíza, Naguabo, Humacao, Vega Baja y Yabucoa.

###

Rep. Hernández Pushes Water Projects for Puerto Rico

Resident Commissioner seeks to secure projects for Corozal, San Juan, and seven municipalities as part of his agenda to prioritize the basics

WASHINGTON, DC — As part of his agenda to prioritize the basics and address the water crisis in Puerto Rico, Resident Commissioner Pablo José Hernández asked the Senate to maintain, in the final version of federal water infrastructure legislation, several projects and priorities for Puerto Rico that have already been approved by the House of Representatives.

The priorities are already included in the House version of the Water Resources Development Act, known as the 2026 Water Resources Development Act (WRDA), which advanced in committee, and Hernández is working to ensure they remain during negotiations with the Senate and make it into the final version.

“My agenda to prioritize the basics is about delivering results on the problems that affect our people every day. Puerto Rico needs better water infrastructure, communities better protected from flooding, and action for our coasts. We are already advancing these priorities in the House, and now I am working to make sure they reach the finish line,” said the Resident Commissioner.

Among the measures the Resident Commissioner seeks to secure are up to $75 million for water and environmental infrastructure projects in Puerto Rico, $10 million for water and sewer infrastructure in Corozal, and new impact studies for the Río Puerto Nuevo flood control project in San Juan, so that the concerns of neighboring communities can be addressed.

He is also advocating for new studies for flood control, coastal protection, and storm damage projects in Ceiba, Fajardo, Loíza, Naguabo, Humacao, Vega Baja, and Yabucoa.

title: Comisionado Residente: ODSEC aguanta millones en fondos federales para combatir la pobreza
text:
CAGUAS, Puerto Rico - El Comisionado Residente de Puerto Rico, Pablo José Hernández envió una carta a la Oficina para el Desarrollo Socioeconómico y Comunitario de Puerto Rico (ODSEC) sobre posibles retrasos en el desembolso y la administración de fondos federales del programa Community Services Block Grant (CSBG), un programa federal que financia organizaciones comunitarias que ayudan a familias de bajos ingresos a conseguir empleo, estudiar y estabilizar su vivienda, entre otras medidas de bienestar social.

ODSEC es la agencia principal responsable de administrar y distribuir más de $29 millones en fondos federales del programa CSBG en Puerto Rico. Durante el año fiscal federal 2023, el programa CSBG brindó servicios a 24,786 personas de bajos ingresos en Puerto Rico, pertenecientes a 17,162 familias. Los servicios financiados produjeron más de 2,300 resultados relacionados con empleo, más de 2,000 resultados educativos y más de 800 resultados vinculados con ingresos, activos y bienestar financiero.

El Comisionado Residente reveló que documentos revisados por su oficina indican que al menos una de las cuatro entidades elegibles que reciben fondos del programa CSBG en Puerto Rico experimentó retrasos significativos en el desembolso inicial correspondiente al año fiscal 2025-2026. En su carta, el comisionado residente solicitó un desglose de las fechas en que ODSEC recibió las asignaciones federales, formalizó los acuerdos de subvención y desembolsó los fondos correspondientes a los años fiscales 2025, 2026 y, si está disponible, 2027. También requirió una explicación de cualquier retraso significativo y de las razones que lo provocaron. El Comisionado Residente solicitó que ODSEC entregue una respuesta escrita completa no más tarde del 26 de septiembre de 2026.

“ODSEC recibe fondos federales para combatir la pobreza y los desembolsa a varias entidades. Hemos recibido quejas de que se están atrasando. Esto afecta a la gente necesitada de Puerto Rico y queremos saber por qué se tardan y ayudar a resolver el problema”, dijo el comisionado residente”.

title: Rep. Houchin Applauds Announcement of Nuclear Microreactor at NWS Crane to Develop Energy Resilience
text:
September 9, 2026

Today, Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09) celebrated the Department of War’s announcement that Naval Weapons Station (NWS) Crane will host Indiana's first advanced nuclear Micro Modular Reactor (MMR), with installation planned no later than September 2028.

The project, executed jointly by the Army's Janus Program, the Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Navy for Energy, Installations and Environment, the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, and the State of Indiana, will deliver reliable, around-the-clock power to one of the nation's premier warfighting innovation hubs.

"Crane is a unique and valuable asset to our National Defense Portfolio and this investment demonstrates that Indiana is at the forefront of unleashing American energy.” said Rep. Houchin. "With proven success in powering submarines, microreactors at our military installations is a natural next step in U.S. energy deployment and rebuilding our nuclear supply chain. The project will also have a positive impact at West Gate due to increased power supply to the base. Thank you to the Department of War, the Navy, our state and federal partners and to everyone whose efforts made this day possible. I am proud to have been part of a chorus of voices advocating for this project and I am proud to be among NWS Crane’s advocates in Washington.”

As the first power-producing nuclear reactor sited in Indiana, the Crane MMR will expand the state's power generation capacity and support the region's long-standing role as a hub for national defense research and manufacturing. The project implements President Trump's Executive Orders on deploying advanced nuclear reactor technologies for national security and reinvigorating the nuclear industrial base.

title: University of Maryland’s Terp Magazine: Steny Hoyer Yields the Floor
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) was featured in the University of Maryland's (UMD) Terp Magazine Fall 2026 edition. Click here to read the story or see below:

STENY HOYER YIELDS THE FLOOR

By John Tucker

September 4, 2026

Sipping a Beer at a Capitol Hill soirée in 1988, John Berry ’80 overheard a congressional staffer mention that a Virginia university was lobbying the National Archives to build a huge facility on its campus to house millions of its documents. The next morning Berry tipped off his boss, U.S. Rep. Steny H. Hoyer ’63, that the prized repository was in play.

Within days, Hoyer and University System of Maryland Chancellor John S. Toll were leading the archivist of the United States on a tour of UMD’s campus; a couple of weeks later, Hoyer added an earmark to an appropriations bill establishing UMD as the site of the eventual 1.8 million-square-foot building. A befuddled Virginia staffer who later ran into Berry said, “I’ve never been so thoroughly sideswiped. Hoyer outsmarted us.”

Hoyer recalls the coup jubilantly: “Now it’s probably the premier archival institution in the world,” he says. “We brought some fantastic researchers to the campus.”

It was a classic move by Hoyer, who will retire from a 45-year career in Congress when his term ends in January. The longest-serving member of either chamber to represent Maryland, Hoyer shaped the influential 5th District abutting Washington into a research powerhouse, helping pump billions of dollars into behemoths like NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Patuxent River Naval Air Station and NOAA Center for Weather and Climate Prediction, many of them tightly aligned with the University of Maryland.

“Steny’s leadership resulted in the modern federal research presence in the state of Maryland,” says emeritus UMD trustee Tim Maloney, a former state delegate whose district overlapped with Hoyer’s. “He did it quietly and without recognition. He was just interested in seeing results.”

The No. 2 member of the Democratic caucus for two decades—second only to Rep. Nancy Pelosi, an ally and frequent sparring partner—Hoyer played the role of happy warrior and shrewd tactician, a consensus-building centrist who complemented her street-fighting progressivism. The 87-year-old has spent nearly his entire career in public office; Hoyer was elected in 1966 to the Maryland Senate and joined the U.S. House of Representatives in 1981.

"[Hoyer] is one of the most underrated giants of U.S. legislative history." John Berry '80 Former Staffer and Ambassador to Australia

Still popular—he won 72% of the vote in his district in the 2024 primary—Hoyer walks away as the only Marylander to serve as majority leader. A throwback to an era when members of both major parties respected each other, he helped steer the passage of bipartisan landmark legislation including the 1990 American with Disabilities Act and the 2002 Help Americas Vote Act in response to the contested 2000 presidential election, the most sweeping election reform since the Voting Rights Act.

“He is one of the most underrated giants of U.S. legislative history,” says Berry, who after working for Hoyer ran President Obama’s Office of Personnel Management and served as ambassador to Australia.

Following retirement, Hoyer will donate his official papers to UMD Libraries, a collection that contains everything from personal notes, speeches, photos, campaign materials and correspondences with constituents and colleagues.

“From the very beginning, the University of Maryland has been a big part of my life, and I’m very proud of it,” he says.

Born in New York, Hoyer moved to District Heights, Md., as a child and enrolled in UMD in 1957 (tuition: $178). After posting 1.7 and 1.0 GPAs his freshman year, he took a semester off, then reenrolled, still without direction.

One day that spring, he was set to leave campus when a Pontiac convertible cruised by, carrying the guest speaker to the annual convocation ceremony. Hoyer thought the car looked cool and decided to follow it.

The teenager sat in awe as the handsome young U.S. senator talked passionately about politics and implored graduates to serve their communities and country. Immediately drawn to public service, Hoyer now calls his walk to the field house to hear John F. Kennedy “my road to Damascus.”

He changed his major from business to government and politics and was elected student government vice president. After marrying his high school sweetheart and graduating with high honors, Hoyer enrolled in Georgetown law school and joined the campaign team of U.S. Rep. Daniel Brewster of Maryland; there, he met a young staffer from Baltimore named Nancy D’Alesandro, who the following year became Nancy Pelosi. After he was elected president of the Maryland Young Democrats, anointed by The Washington Post as “a man to watch” and remained on staff when Brewster became a U.S. senator, he made his first run for elected office, distinguishing himself in a crowded field vying for a state Senate seat with a platform on fair housing.

The newly drawn district had backed segregationist candidate George Wallace in the 1964 presidential election, but Hoyer focused on a concentration of Black constituents, knocking on doors till his knuckles hurt. “People saw a skinny white kid looking younger than my 26 years, and said, ‘What are you doing here?’” he recalls. He won Black voters’ support nearly 7-to-1 and claimed the seat by 300 votes. In Annapolis, he cast one of his first votes to end the ban on interracial marriage.

At 35, he became Maryland’s youngest-ever Senate president, championing a district growing increasingly Black, educated, affluent and attractive to federal government workers. In 1981 he won a special election to represent the U.S. House’s 5th District, earning the nickname Boy Wonder.

“There was a certain way Steny Hoyer’s heels click-clicked along the marble halls of the State House that set him apart from the others. He had the sharpest, most urgent click-click in Annapolis,” the Post wrote upon his departure from the legislature.

Among his new constituents was Yvette Lewis, a Prince George’s County music teacher who dreamed of singing professionally—if only she could get her foot in the door at the Kennedy Center. Her husband suggested she call her congressman; maybe she could speak with a staffer. With surprising ease, she secured a meeting with Hoyer. She left with a smile and no expectations, but two weeks later received a letter from the Kennedy Center offering an interview.

Lewis landed a Kennedy Center teaching job, then a Washington Opera audition, then a resident understudy position. Following the contentious 2000 presidential election, she became politically active and ultimately served as chair of the Maryland Democratic Party for eight years. “Steny Hoyer changed my life,” she says.

Hoyer didn’t remember their original meeting when they first bumped into each other in political circles years later, but that didn’t surprise her.

“I’m not unique,” says Lewis, now a close friend who sits on the University System of Maryland Board of Regents. “I’m one of a million Hoyer stories.”

Hoyer gradually built his influence in Congress, chairing the Helsinki Commission on U.S.-European security, earning a seat on the powerful House Appropriations Committee and traveling to Darfur and South Sudan to raise awareness of genocide. He became Pelosi’s chief lieutenant in 2003 and House majority leader in 2007, charged with scheduling floor business and mobilizing the party vote on important legislation.

With increased clout, he directed millions of dollars into UMD programs through federal agency appropriations. A savvy analyst, he identified potential research partnerships, joint faculty appointments and student pipelines connecting UMD to the government, then brokered behind-the-scenes deals.

“He might tell his colleagues in the House, ‘Hey, the engineering school’s developing a remote sensing program that would be great for NASA Goddard,’” says Brian Darmody, chief strategy officer for the Association of University Research Parks. Formerly UMD’s assistant vice president for research and economic development, he worked closely with Hoyer in the 2000s to establish M Square, a public-private research hub that has since grown into UMD’s Discovery District Maryland.

Hoyer also secured funds from the Department of Defense for a UMD center now known as the Applied Research Lab for Intelligence and Security; from the Department of Agriculture for the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center, where more than two dozen UMD faculty work; and from the Food and Drug Administration for its Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition, which has a research partnership with UMD in College Park. On campus, Hoyer also helped net construction money for the Physical Sciences Complex and The Clarice Smith Performing Arts Center.

Meanwhile, he continued preaching in support of civil rights. In 2010, when a bill to end the “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” policy banning gay Americans from serving openly in the military died in committee, Hoyer sidestepped the blockade by orchestrating a second Senate vote at the eleventh hour of the session, a “political miracle,” says Berry, his former staffer.

Hoyer was the first person whom Berry came out to as gay, after his parents. When Berry’s partner died of AIDS, Hoyer pulled over on Route 50 and listened to him weep on the phone for 30 minutes.

“He’s not only the best boss I’ve ever had, but a mentor, a second father, a true saint,” says Berry.

Hoyer looks younger han his 87 years, and he knows it. “God’s been good,” he says, after practically bounding into his office on the top floor of the Longworth building in crisp shirtsleeves and a yellow tie. Mentally sharp, though unsure whether he could deliver at 89, he is retiring somewhat reluctantly. Pelosi, his longtime colleague, is also stepping down at age 86.

One corner of Hoyer’s office is dedicated to the late Rep. John Lewis, one of his closest friends in Congress, with whom he marched 15 times across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Ala., to make good trouble. In an opposite corner is the flag of Denmark (the self-described “proud Dane” in 2009 was honored as a Knight of the Order of the Dannebrog).

After retirement, he’ll remain active in Democratic politics and spend more time in his St. Mary’s County home. A rabid UMD football and basketball fan, he intends to keep shouting at nearly every home game alongside his wife, Elaine Kamarck, a director at a public policy nonprofit whom he married in 2023. (Hoyer’s first wife, the educator Judy Pickett Hoyer, died in 1997, leading Hoyer to create early-childhood programs across Maryland in her name.)

He’ll leave the House having shaped the careers of hundreds of staffers, including Jazz Lewis ’11, MPP ’14, who met Hoyer as a graduate student intending to become a community organizer. Instead, he agreed to lead his reelection campaign the day after commencement.

“His approach to public service was kindness, thoughtfulness and always following up. Every function was super long because he listened to everyone—it didn’t matter if they were a mechanic or someone’s granny,” says Lewis, who became Hoyer’s senior policy adviser and is now UMD’s director of state government relations.

Hoyer’s seat will almost certainly be inherited by another recent campaign manager, 32-year-old state Del. Adrian Boafo, who in June won the Democratic primary.

Ever congenial, the lion of the House laments that American politics has devolved into pettiness and divisiveness over the last decade. Still, he’s an optimist, easily quoting from Kennedy’s 1961 inaugural address: “The torch has been passed to a new generation of Americans ... unwilling to witness or permit the slow undoing of those human rights to which this nation has always been committed.”

Twelve presidential administrations later, in an emotional January speech on the House floor to announce his retirement, Hoyer passed his own torch, urging his colleagues to examine their conscience and renew their courage: “We must remember that we are not great or unique because we say we’re great, but because we are just, generous and fair.”

"I believe in democracy. I believe that over time, people mostly do the right thing." Steny Hoyer '63

title: Over 250 Current & Former Members of Congress Urge Supreme Court to Block Trump’s Executive Order Limiting Mail Voting
text:
Washington, D.C. — Current and former Members of Congress mobilized in a court filing challenging the legality of President Donald Trump’s Executive Order seeking to exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The effort was led by House Administration Ranking Member Joe Morelle; Assistant House Minority Leader Joe Neguse, who leads the House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force; and Task Force Co-Chairs Oversight Ranking Member Robert Garcia and Judiciary Ranking Member Jamie Raskin. In the Senate, the brief was championed by Rules Committee Ranking Member Alex Padilla; Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer; Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin; and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gary Peters.

The group, made up of a bipartisan, bicameral coalition of 261 lawmakers, filed an amicus brief to the Supreme Court of the United States in the matter of United States Postal Service, et al., v. State of California, et al., a lawsuit brought by a coalition of State Attorneys General against the U.S. Postal Service. The court case challenges a Final Rule issued by the USPS pursuant to Trump’s directive that imposes unconstitutional and unworkable restrictions on mail-in voting, including requiring states to provide a “citizenship verification list” and attempting to give USPS control over who can vote by mail.

One-third of Americans are expected to vote by mail in the upcoming midterm elections—a voting practice Donald Trump himself used as recently as August 2026, when the president voted in Florida’s Republican primary.

In the court filing, the amici curiae argue that Trump’s Executive Order 14399, “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections,” violates the separation of powers and usurps congressional authorities outlined in Article I of the U.S. Constitution, which gives the states and Congress exclusive authority over election administration.

“As current and former legislators, amici took an oath to uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States—including its guarantee of the separation of powers. Amici have a particular interest in defending the institutional role of the Legislative Branch under Article I of the Constitution and in vindicating the long-settled principle that the Constitution commits ultimate regulatory authority over federal elections to Congress. The Constitution does not contemplate the Executive Branch acting unilaterally to assert power over federal elections. Yet that is what the Order and Final Rule do,” wrote the lawmakers.

The amici also pointed to a recent federal court ruling blocking the USPS from implementing its newly finalized mail ballot rule for the midterm elections, saying the agency lacked the authority to implement the rule and that its actions are “substantively unconstitutional and contrary to law.”

“The district court correctly concluded that Appellees are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims that USPS lacked authority to issue the Final Rule, that the Final Rule unconstitutionally imposes mail-ballot requirements on the States, and that the Final Rule unconstitutionally bars non-compliant State and local election officials from using the USPS to mail ballots at all.”

The group concluded by asserting States’ power to administer elections and Congress’s power to make or alter rules regulating elections, which the Supreme Court itself has described as an “override” authority. The president’s illegal incursion on this authority is an attempt to disenfranchise people who depend on mail-in ballots to vote.

The lawmakers concluded: “The integrity of our constitutional system depends on each branch keeping to its assigned role. The Framers set up a two-part system that gave the States default authority to regulate federal elections subject to Congress’s authority to override the States. The Framers did not provide the President with any authority to interfere in that system, nor has Congress imbued the Executive Branch with any such authority by statute.”

title: Kaptur Announces $3.75 Million of Investment in Programs to Support Northwest Ohio Fathers
text:
Toledo, OH — Today, Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09), a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, announced that three Northwest Ohio organizations will receive awards totaling $3.75 Million through the US Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Family Assistance, through its Responsible Fatherhood Program. The Zepf Center, the Ridge Project, Inc., and Pathway, Inc. will each receive $1,250,000 for their programs that encourage fathers in our Northwest Ohio community to take an active role in their children’s lives.

"Our Northwest Ohio community is fortunate to have amazing people and programs that work to build strong families and caring communities,” said Congresswoman Kaptur. “Equipping young fathers with the skills and resources they need to be an active presence in their families’ lives will lay a solid foundation for success. The vital work these organizations do cannot be overstated, and this major Federal investment means that thousands of our region’s youngest citizens will grow up with positive role models and the ability to foster healthy lifelong relationships.”

The Zepf Center will use the award for their Fatherhood Connection program, which seeks to empower fathers at every stage of parenthood, from expecting fathers to grandfathers and father figures. They teachparenting classes through the Nurturing Fathers program, and they provide extensive economic and vocational support to fathers. The Ridge Project serves families navigating the justice system, whether a member of the family is incarcerated or on probation. Their award will support its TYRO Fathers program, which equips fathers with life, job, and parenting skills for becoming strongly involved in their families’ lives. Serving the Toledo-area community, Pathway provides numerous services to reduce poverty. They serve families, seniors, and individuals with disabilities, and their award will be used to support their Brothers United program.

These new Federal investments build on similar previous awards to communities across our Northwest Ohio region. Just last year, Congresswoman Kaptur secured a combined total of more than $3.7 Million for three responsible fatherhood programs through the US Department of Health and Human Services.

title: Congressman Langworthy Announces $500,000 Federal Grant to Strengthen Hornell-Area Wastewater Infrastructure
text:
Washington, D.C.--September 9th… Congressman Nick Langworthy today announced that the City of Hornell has been awarded $500,000 in federal funding from the Appalachian Regional Commission (ARC) to advance a major regional wastewater infrastructure project serving the Hornell area municipalities including Hornell, North Hornell, and Hornellsville.

The ARC grant will support the engineering and design phase of the Hornell Intermunicipal Sewer Improvement Project, a collaborative effort between the City of Hornell, Village of North Hornell and Town of Hornellsville. The project has a total cost of $1,082,700, with an additional $582,700 in state funding.

The federal investment will fund field surveys, subsurface investigations, hydraulic evaluations, environmental reviews, regulatory coordination and the development of preliminary and final engineering documents needed to move the project toward construction. The engineering work will focus on developing construction-ready plans and specifications to replace or rehabilitate eight aging sewer pump stations and associated trunk sewer infrastructure that have exceeded their useful life and are experiencing capacity, reliability and resiliency deficiencies.

“Reliable infrastructure is the foundation for strong communities and a growing economy, and this federal investment will help Hornell and its neighboring communities address critical wastewater needs while laying the groundwork for future growth,” said Congressman Langworthy. “I’m proud to see federal resources coming back to the Southern Tier to support infrastructure that protects public health, strengthens our communities, and helps create an environment where businesses can invest and jobs can grow.”

Hornell Mayor John Buckley said, “We are grateful to Congressman Langworthy for his continued efforts to bring federal dollars home to Hornell and the Southern Tier. We appreciate Congressman Langworthy’s partnership and his commitment to making sure communities like ours have a strong advocate in Washington.”

The Appalachian Regional Commission is a federal-state partnership serving 423 counties across the Appalachian region. Its mission is to strengthen economic growth and build community capacity throughout Appalachia.

title: Malliotakis, Officials Join Family To Highlight Father Vincent Capodanno’s Life & Path to Sainthood
text:
(STATEN ISLAND, NY) — Today, Congresswoman Nicole Malliotakis (NY-11) held a press conference to highlight the extraordinary courage, faith, and selflessness of Father Vincent Capodanno, a U.S. Navy priest who sacrificed his life serving wounded Marines during the Vietnam War and was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor for his extraordinary heroism.
